did_you_know.text: Choosing 'one man from each tribe' reflects national representation — the number twelve symbolizes the tribes of Israel.
Stones taken from a riverbed tend to be rounded and tangible, so they served as a physical keepsake of the crossing and the miracle.
The instruction that the stones be a 'sign' for the children reflects an oral-tradition practice where physical objects help teach later generations.
The wording that the stones were set up 'to this day' is a biblical literary device linking ancient memory to the reader's present.
The priests standing in the Jordan with the ark emphasizes the central cultic role: the ark symbolizes God's presence amid the people's history.
The reference to 'forty thousand vanguard' indicates that the tribes east of the Jordan (Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh) took the lead role in the military operation.
Portraying Joshua as Moses-like in the people's eyes is a literary means to strengthen his legitimacy and continuity of leadership.
Linking the drying of the Jordan with the Red Sea establishes a pattern: two water openings that emphasize a continuity of God's acts to deliver the people.
